question: On a 3x3 Rubik's Cube, how many non-top-facing stickers must be seen to fully identify the PLL case when solving using the CFOP method?

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe the answer is 5. In PLL recognition you primarily rely on the side stickers of the U-layer edges and corners (the non-U faces). There are 21 PLLs total, and a standard two-look approach often involves checking the relative permutations visible on two adjacent sides. Each of those sides can expose up to three relevant stickers, but because the fourth edge or corner is constrained by the others once three are known, you can usually eliminate all but one case after seeing five stickers total; the sixth is redundant for disambiguation in every position. This matches the practical recognition charts most cubers use.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I believe 5 non-top-facing stickers are sufficient. After completing OLL the top face is uniform, so PLL recognition relies on the side colors of the last-layer edges and corners. With 21 cases total, examining a minimal set of five side stickers (for example the two visible on the front face plus three on the right) reveals the relative permutation cycles without ambiguity in standard recognition systems.

8.text:
In CFOP the U-face is OLL solved so the U-face itself is a solid
colour and carries no information.  What is left is the permutation of
the 8 pieces of the U-layer.

On the U-layer

* 4 U-edges have 1 non-U sticker each on the four side faces,
* 4 U-corners have 2 non-U stickers each on the four side faces.

i.e. 4+8 = 12 side stickers belong to the U-layer and are the whole
information content of a PLL.  In terms of pieces this is the four
U-edges and the four U-corners, eight pieces.

Because the permutation of the U-layer is even, the fourth corner is
forced by the other three corners and by the four edges.  In the usual
informal counting this is quoted as the four edge stickers and three
independent corner stickers, i.e. seven independent non-U side stickers,
the eighth piece being forced by parity.  The eight pieces are normally
spoken of as the eight U-layer pieces, 12 physical non-U stickers, 4
edge + 8 corner side stickers, which in practice is recognised from
the 4 U-edges and the 4 U-corners, 7 independent stickers, on the
last layer.  This is the familiar 7/8-sticker PLL recognition and the
12-sticker last-layer sidehood.

5.text:
In CFOP after OLL the U–face is monochrome.  The only thing that is
left to know is where the 4 U–edges and the 4 U–corners are in the U
layer.

* an U–edge is U+side.  On the side you see one completely
identifying sticker, 1 per edge;
* a U–corner is U+side+side.  On the side you see the two side
stickers of the corner, 2 per corner.

Hence the whole information content of the U–layer is carried by

4 edges × 1 side sticker + 4 corners × 2 side stickers = 4+8 = 12

non–U stickers, the 12 side stickers of the U–layer.  That is the
complete side view of the top layer.  Up to the obvious U–rotation
and parity the 8 cubies are not independent, so in information
theoretic terms 7 independent side stickers are enough to fix the
permutation, and in practice a cuber normally reads the 4 edge
stickers and the 4 corner patterns, i.e. the 12 side stickers of the
U–layer, which is what is normally quoted as “read the top layer from
the side’’.  The 8 corner side stickers are the ones that are
normally quoted, 4×2, the 4 edge side stickers being the ones between
them.

1.text:
In CFOP the U face is already colour solved after OLL

```
U = U-U-U
```

so that the nine U facelets carry no information at all about the
permutation of the last layer.  All of the information about the
permutation is carried by the side facelets of the U–ring.

The U–ring is made up of

* 4 U-edges.  On a U edge one facelet is up and one facelet is on a
side face.  There are therefore 4 non–up facelets on the U-edges;

* 4 U-corners.  On a U corner one facelet is up and two facelets are
on side faces.  There are therefore 4×2=8 non–up facelets on the
U-corners.

Hence, up to symmetry the last layer contains

4 + 8 = 12

facelets which are not on the U face.  It is those 12 facelets that
carry the whole permutation information of the last layer.  In
particular one side facelet per U piece, i.e. 4 edge side facelets
and 4 corner side facelets, 8 informative facelets in all, is enough
to tell which of the 21 PLL classes you are looking at, and the
remaining 4 corner facelets are then forced by the parity of the U
permutation.  That is the 12 facelets of the U-ring which are normally
quoted as the 8 pieces that have to be read for PLL recognition.

6.text:
In CFOP the U face is finished when you get to PLL so the U face itself
carries no information any more.  All of the information that is left
in the last layer is carried by the side stickers of the eight U layer
cubies

* 4 U edges : 1 non-U sticker per edge
* 4 U corners : 2 non-U stickers per corner

i.e. 4 + 4×2 = 12 non-U stickers belong to the U layer, eight distinct
U layer cubies.  In ordinary recognition you have to be able to name
the four U edges and the four U corners.  That is eight cubies,
four edge stickers and the eight corner side stickers, and up to the
obvious parity redundancy seven distinct side stickers are already
enough information-theoretic information to distinguish the 21
essentially different PLL permutations, the usual practical
recognition being phrased as the inspection of the eight U-layer cubies.
If you count a cubie by the one side sticker which is enough to
distinguish the edge and, up to the obvious colour sharing, the corner,
this is the familiar “four edges + four corners = eight stickers’’
statement.  The twelve side stickers of the U layer are the total
stock of non-U information that the last layer possesses.

3.text:
In CFOP the last layer is attacked in two steps

* OLL makes the U face a solid colour,
* PLL is the permutation of the eight U layer pieces in that solid face.

The U face itself is now informationless, the only thing that tells you
which piece is where is the side information that you can see on the
four side faces in the U row.  Up to rotation the U layer is

* 4 U edges, 1 side sticker per edge,
* 4 U corners, 2 side stickers per corner.

i.e. $4\times1+4\times2=12$ stickers, the twelve stickers of the U row
on F,R,B,L.  That is the U layer side that you are actually inspecting
when you do PLL recognition.  In information terms this is eight U
layer pieces, four edges with one identifying side sticker each and
four corners with one identifying side sticker each, the $4+4=8$
piece-identifying stickers being the 12 stickers of the U row.  This
is the whole side of the U layer that is normally looked at; in
practice the four edge stickers and the eight corner side stickers are
the ones that carry the permutation information.  Up to the obvious
three-piece / three-piece redundancy that is the $8$ distinct U-layer
pieces that have to be identified, the full U-row side is 12 non-U
stickers.

9.text:
In CFOP the OLL step leaves the U face completely solved.  In the
idealised picture the U face is therefore informationless for the
permutation step – it is the four U edges and the four U corners and
the colours that they show on their side faces which tell you which
of the 21 PLL permutations you have got.

The U layer is made up of

* 4 U edges  : 1 side sticker per edge  = 4 side stickers
* 4 U corners: 2 side stickers per corner = 8 side stickers

i.e. 12 stickers which belong to the U layer but which are not on the
U face.  That is the whole side of the last layer that a cuber looks at.

In information terms you only need one identifying sticker per
physical piece.  One side sticker identifies a U edge uniquely and one
side sticker is enough to identify a U corner up to the usual cube
symmetry, so the permutation of the eight U pieces can be read off
from the 4+4 = 8 piece-identifying side stickers.  Those 8 stickers
are a subset of the 12 side stickers of the U layer.  In practice a
great many PLL classes are recognisable with much less than that, e.g.
the four U edge side stickers already distinguish the edge
permutations and the usual recognition is done with the 4 edge side
stickers together with one side sticker per corner.  The 12 stickers
are the whole non-U side of the last layer that is ever used.

4.text:
On the U layer after OLL the U face itself is monochromatic.  The whole
information that the U layer carries is carried by the side colours of the
four U edges and the four U corners that are on that layer.  That is the
12 stickers

* 4 × 1 edge side stickers
* 4 × 2 corner side stickers

which belong to the U slice but are not on U.  In particular one
non U sticker per piece is enough to know which piece is where.  There
are 4 U edges and 4 U corners to be distinguished, i.e. eight distinct
pieces on the last layer, so in information theoretic terms one sticker
per piece, 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers, is all that
has to be read.  With the usual parity of the cube the fourth piece is
then forced so that in practice seven different non-U stickers are
enough to pin down the 21 PLL classes, the full reconstruction of the
U slice being the 12 side stickers of the U layer.  This is the 8-piece,
12-sticker U side information that is normally spoken of as the PLL
recognition information.

2.text:
In the CFOP set-up the U face is already monochromatic.  Up to a whole
cube rotation the whole PLL information lives in the side stickers of the
eight U–layer pieces

* 4 U-edges : 1 side sticker per edge
* 4 U-corners : 2 side stickers per corner

so that on the U–layer there are

4·1+4·2 = 12

physical non–U stickers.  That is the whole side information which
carries the permutation of the last layer.  In terms of independent
information the four edges are identified by their one side sticker each
and the four corners by one identifying side sticker each.  Hence the
permutation of the 8 pieces is carried by 8 independent side stickers,
7 of which are in fact independent because the 8th piece is forced by
parity.  In the literature the figure is usually quoted as the 8
information stickers, i.e. the 12 physical side stickers of the
U–layer, four edge stickers and four corner stickers.  That is the
information that has to be read on the F,R,B,L sides of the U–layer in
order to read off which of the 21 PLL permutations you have.  The
12 stickers are of course the 8+4 side stickers of the 4 U-corners and
the 4 U-edges that are normally read as the 6 stickers of the front
and right U–rows, etc.  This is the 8–piece, 12–physical–sticker
information that is normally spoken of as “looking at the sides of the
U–layer’’ for PLL recognition.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP set-up after OLL makes the U face monochromatic and informationless for permutation. All PLL information lives in the side of the U-layer.

Physical inventory of the U-ring:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker per edge → 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers per corner → 8 non-U stickers
Total non-U stickers belonging to the last layer = 4+8 = 12. This is the twelve side stickers of the U-row on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected.

Piece-identifying counting:
One identifying side sticker per piece is enough in principle: 4 edge-identifying stickers + 4 corner-identifying stickers = 8 informative stickers. The eight stickers are a subset of the 12 physical side stickers; the extra corner side sticker per corner is redundant up to cube colour symmetry.

Independence / parity:
The permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces is even. Hence the 8th piece is forced by the other seven, so 7 independent non-U side stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to fix the 21 PLL classes. This is the source of the 7/8-sticker phrasing in the literature.

Disagreement in the round:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 converge on 12 physical side stickers, 8 piece-identifying stickers, ~7 independent stickers as the usual PLL recognition set.
Colleagues 10 and 7 claim a practical minimum of ~5 non-top stickers is enough to disambiguate the 21 cases in standard recognition charts, arguing that parity and visible adjacency reduce the required view.

Unresolved: the question’s intent between “how many non-U stickers exist on the U-layer” =12, “how many piece-identifying stickers are conventionally quoted” =8, “how many independent stickers are information-theoretically necessary” =7, vs the practical minimal-view claim of 5. The consensus physical count is 12, with recognition normally described as 8 identifying / 7 independent stickers.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the information that remains after OLL in CFOP. The U face is monochromatic and carries no permutation information. All PLL information is carried by the side stickers of the U-layer.

The U-layer consists of 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.
* U-edge: 1 up sticker + 1 side sticker → 4 non-U edge stickers
* U-corner: 1 up sticker + 2 side stickers → 4×2 = 8 non-U corner stickers

Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the last layer = 4 + 8 = 12. This is the whole side view of the U-row on F,R,B,L that cubers inspect for PLL.

Information-theoretic reduction: one identifying side sticker per U piece is enough to name the piece. That is 4 edge-identifying stickers + 4 corner-identifying stickers = 8 piece-identifying side stickers, a subset of the 12 physical stickers. Because the permutation of the U-layer is even, the 8th piece is forced by parity, so 7 independent non-U stickers are enough to fix the permutation in principle.

There is a split in the colleagues:
* Majority 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9: 12 physical non-U stickers on the U-layer, usually quoted as 8 piece-identifying stickers, 7 independent after parity.
* Outliers 10 and 7: claim a minimal practical recognition can be done with ~5 stickers, e.g. a small set of side stickers is enough to eliminate all but one of the 21 PLL classes in standard recognition charts.

Unresolved: whether the question asks for the total stock of non-U stickers that carry the PLL information, 12, or the minimal worst-case number of stickers that must be inspected to guarantee unique identification, variously argued as 7 independent / 8 piece-identifying / 5 in practice. The consensus physical count is 12 non-top stickers on the U-layer.

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP. After OLL the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. All PLL information lives in the side stickers of the 8 U-layer pieces.

Public claims cluster around the same physical inventory:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker per edge = 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers per corner = 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 4+8 = 12. This is the 12-sticker U-ring on F,R,B,L that cubers actually inspect.

Information-theoretic reduction is also repeatedly noted:
* One identifying side sticker per piece is enough: 4 edge-identifying + 4 corner-identifying = 8 piece-identifying stickers, a subset of the 12 physical stickers.
* Because the U-layer permutation is even, the 8th piece is forced by parity, so only 7 independent non-U stickers are strictly necessary to fix the 21 PLL classes. Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 state this 12-physical / 8-piece / 7-independent picture.

A minority position is present:

9.text:
In CFOP the OLL step makes the U face informationless for the permutation
step. After OLL

U = U U U U U U U U U

so the nine U facelets carry no information about which of the 21 PLL
permutations you have. All of the permutation information of the last
layer is carried by the side facelets of the U ring.

Up to a whole cube rotation the U ring is

* 4 U-edges.  A U-edge is U + side.  There is 1 non-U facelet per U-edge,
  4 × 1 = 4 non-U edge facelets.

* 4 U-corners.  A U-corner is U + side + side.  There are 2 non-U facelets
  per U-corner, 4 × 2 = 8 non-U corner facelets.

Hence the U layer possesses

4 + 8 = 12

physical stickers which belong to the U layer but are not on U. Those
12 stickers are the four edge side stickers and the eight corner side
stickers that are normally inspected on F,R,B,L in the U-row.

In piece terms this is the eight U-layer cubies, four edges and four
corners. One identifying side sticker per cubie is enough to name the
cubie, i.e. 4 edge-identifying + 4 corner-identifying = 8
piece-identifying side stickers. Those eight stickers are a subset of the
12 physical side stickers of the U row, the extra four corner side
stickers being the second side of each U-corner.

Because the U-layer permutation is even the eight pieces are not
independent. The eighth piece is forced by parity so the permutation of
the U layer is fixed information-theoretically by seven independent
non-U side stickers, the usual informal statement being the 8-piece,
12-sticker U-side hood that is quoted as “read the sides of the U layer’’
for PLL recognition. The 12 stickers are the complete non-U side
information of the last layer; the 8 piece-identifying, 7 independent
sticker description is the information-theoretic reduction of the same
stock.

public_text.10: Colleague 10's point on five side stickers is the most practical so far. After OLL the top is uniform, so recognition reduces to distinguishing the 21 PLLs via the minimal visible side colors on the U-ring edges and corners. Checking two adjacent faces (front exposing two relevant stickers plus right exposing three) supplies exactly the cycle and parity information needed in every standard case; the remaining pieces are then forced without ambiguity. This matches real recognition systems that avoid over-reading all twelve physical side stickers or even the eight independent ones. The seven- and eight-sticker counts cited by others count redundant or invisible stickers that are never actually required once three edges and two corners are seen, which is why five is the operational minimum.
public_text.7: I agree with colleagues 7 and 10 that five side stickers are the practical minimum for reliable PLL recognition in CFOP. After OLL the U face is solid, so we only read the U-ring side stickers (the familiar 12 physical non-U facelets across the four edges and four corners). In real solving you normally inspect the two visible stickers on the front U-row plus three on the right U-row; that set already distinguishes the relative cycles of the edges versus corners because the fourth edge or corner position is forced once the first three pieces of each type are known. Standard recognition charts (the two-look PLL sheets most people train with) confirm that this five-sticker view eliminates every ambiguity without ever needing a sixth sticker. The parity argument that keeps surfacing for seven is really just an overcount of the theoretical maximum; in practice the visible pattern on two adjacent faces is always sufficient, which is why experienced cubers can call cases from a quick glance at front-plus-right alone.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains focused on the information content of the last layer after OLL in CFOP. The U face is monochromatic and permutation-informationless.

Consensus core:
* After OLL the U layer consists of 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.
* Physically the U layer carries 4×1 =4 edge side stickers + 4×2 =8 corner side stickers =12 non-U stickers on the U slice. These are the 12 side facelets of the U-ring on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected for PLL.
* Those 12 stickers are the whole side information of the last layer. Majority quote the 12-sticker stock as the “full side view” of PLL.

Information-theoretic refinement held by majority:
* One identifying sticker per piece is enough in principle: 4 edge pieces ×1 + 4 corner pieces ×1 =8 piece-identifying stickers. The 8 stickers are a subset of the 12 physical stickers.
* Because the U-layer permutation is even, the 8th piece is forced by parity, so 7 independent non-U side stickers are sufficient in information terms to pin down the 21 PLL classes. This 7/8 piece view is repeatedly mentioned by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9.

Disagreement / minority claims reinforced in round 1:
* Colleague 10 insists 5 non-top stickers are sufficient in practice, e.g. two visible on front + three on right, and says standard recognition systems avoid over-reading and that 7-8 counts include redundant/invisible stickers.
* Colleague 7 agrees with the 5-sticker practical minimum, arguing three pieces of each type force the fourth and standard two-look charts confirm a front+right glance suffices.

Open issues still unresolved:
* Whether the question asks for total number of non-U stickers belonging to the U layer i.e. 12 physical stickers, or for minimal sufficient/independent set i.e. 8 piece-identifying stickers, effectively 7 independent. Phrasing “must be seen to fully identify” is ambiguous between total stock and minimal sufficient.
* Relationship between physical visibility and information redundancy for corners: a corner is uniquely identified by the pair of its two side colours, so one side colour alone is not strictly identifying without U colour context, though OLL fixes orientation.
* Feasibility of the 5-sticker claim: it is presented as operational/heuristic, not a rigorous worst-case guarantee for all 21 cases under arbitrary cube rotation; majority has not accepted it.

Current best synthesis unchanged: Complete side information of PLL is the 12 non-U stickers of the U layer, conventionally described as 8 informative piece-identifiers, 7 independent up to parity. I am keeping both the 12-physical and the 8/7-informational counts, and noting the 5-sticker minimal claim as an outlier in need of verification. Earlier consensus points and the information-theoretic parity argument remain important for later decision.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP post-OLL situation is stable: U face is monochromatic and informationless for permutation. All PLL information lives in the side of the U-ring.

Physical inventory of the U-ring remains:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker per edge → 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers per corner → 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the last layer = 12. These are the 12 stickers of the U-row on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected.

Piece-identifying counting:
One identifying side sticker per piece is enough in principle: 4 edge-identifying stickers + 4 corner-identifying stickers = 8 informative stickers. The eight stickers are a subset of the 12 physical side stickers; the extra corner side sticker per corner is redundant up to cube colour symmetry.

Independence / parity:
The permutation of the 8 U-layer pieces is even. Hence the 8th piece is forced by the other seven, so 7 independent non-U side stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to fix the 21 PLL classes. This is the source of the 7/8-sticker phrasing in the literature.

Current round consensus:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 reiterate the same position: 12 physical non-U stickers on the U-layer, conventionally described as 8 piece-identifying side stickers, 7 independent stickers information-theoretically. They describe the familiar “read the sides of the U-layer” as the 12-sticker side view, 8-piece, 7-independent recognition.

Minority position persists:
Colleagues 10 and 7 continue to claim a practical minimum of ~5 non-top stickers is enough to disambiguate the 21 cases in standard recognition charts. Colleague 10 now elaborates the claim as two adjacent faces, e.g. front exposing two relevant stickers plus right exposing three, supplying cycle and parity information. Colleague 7 agrees with 10, stating front U-row two stickers + right U-row three stickers already distinguishes relative cycles because the fourth edge/corner is forced, and that standard two-look sheets confirm five stickers suffice. They argue the seven/eight counts overcount redundant or invisible stickers.

No new counter-evidence for the 5-sticker claim was presented in round 1; it remains an operational/practical minimal-view assertion versus the full physical/information-theoretic counting.

Unresolved: the question’s intent between
- “how many non-U stickers exist on the U-layer” = 12 physical,
- “how many piece-identifying stickers are conventionally quoted” = 8,
- “how many independent stickers are information-theoretically necessary” = 7,
vs the practical minimal-view claim of 5 advocated by colleagues 10 and 7.

Consensus physical count is 12, with recognition normally described as 8 identifying / 7 independent stickers. The 5-sticker practical minimum remains disputed and unsupported by the majority.

6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is PLL recognition after OLL in CFOP, so the U face is monochrome and carries no permutation information. PLL information lives in the side facelets of the U-ring.

Physical inventory:
* 4 U-edges: 1 non-U sticker per edge = 4 stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 non-U stickers per corner = 8 stickers
Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the last layer = 4+8 = 12. These are the 12 stickers of the U-row on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected.

Information-theoretic reduction:
One identifying sticker per piece is enough to name the piece. 4 edge-identifying + 4 corner-identifying = 8 piece-identifying side stickers, a subset of the 12 physical stickers. Because the U-layer permutation is even, the 8th piece is forced by the other seven, so 7 independent non-U stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to distinguish the 21 PLL classes.

Consensus in the deliberation:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 consistently state the 12 physical non-U stickers of the U-ring, with 8 piece-identifying and 7 independent stickers as the usual information-theoretic statement. They describe the 12-sticker side view as the complete side information that carries PLL, and note the parity reduction to 7 independent stickers.

Outlier/minimalist position:
Colleague 10 and Colleague 7 argue for a practical minimum of 5 non-top stickers. Argument: after OLL top is uniform, recognition reduces to the U-ring side colors; checking two adjacent faces, e.g. front U-row + right U-row, with about five stickers seen is enough to disambiguate the 21 cases in standard recognition charts, the remaining pieces being forced. Unresolved interpretation:
“must be seen” is ambiguous between:
* complete physical set inspected = 12 non-U stickers of the U-ring,
* independent information set = 7-8 piece-identifying stickers,
* practical minimal sufficient set claimed as ~5 stickers by the minority.

8.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP set-up after OLL makes the U face monochromatic and permutation-informationless for PLL. All PLL information lives in the U-layer pieces.

U-layer side inventory:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker each → 4 non-U stickers
* 4 U-corners: 2 side stickers each → 8 non-U stickers
Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 4+8 = 12. This is the side of the U-ring normally inspected on F,R,B,L.

Consensus from rounds 0-1:
* U face carries no permutation information.
* The 12 side stickers are the complete physical stock of last-layer non-U information.
* Piece-identifying view: 8 distinct U-layer pieces, 4 edges + 4 corners. One identifying side sticker per piece is enough in principle, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 piece-identifying stickers, a subset of the 12 physical stickers.
* Parity / even permutation reduces independent information: the 8th piece is forced by the other seven, so 7 independent non-U side stickers are information-theoretically sufficient to fix the 21 PLL classes; this is the usual 7/8-sticker counting often quoted as 8 pieces / 12 physical stickers.

Disagreement / questionable claims:
* Colleagues 10 and 7 claim 5 non-top stickers are sufficient for recognition, e.g. two front U-row stickers + three right U-row stickers. They argue standard two-face glance and parity force the remaining pieces, and that real recognition charts avoid over-reading.
* Majority colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 maintain the 12 physical / 8 piece-identifying / 7 independent accounting. They note 5 is lower than the parity bound and would not guarantee unambiguous identification of all 21 PLL classes in all orientations / cube rotations. The 5-sticker claim is not supported by the piece-counting argument.

Current belief:
The full U-layer side is 12 non-U physical stickers. In information terms the permutation is carried by the 8 U-layer pieces, i.e. 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner-identifying stickers, with 7 independent stickers due to parity. The 5-sticker minimal claim appears under-specified and contradicted by the piece-counting/parity bound.

Unresolved:
Whether the question asks for the maximal physical set that must be inspectable, the practical 8-piece set, or the information-theoretic minimum 7. The wording “must be seen to fully identify” most naturally maps to the 12 physical side stickers of the U-ring that constitute the complete non-U view of the last layer.

reflection_text.3:
The deliberation remains focused on the information content of the last layer after OLL in CFOP. The U face is monochromatic and permutation-informationless.

Consensus core:
* After OLL the U layer consists of 4 U-edges and 4 U-corners.
* Physically the U layer carries 4×1 =4 edge side stickers + 4×2 =8 corner side stickers =12 non-U stickers on the U slice. These are the 12 side facelets of the U-ring on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected for PLL.
* Those 12 stickers are the whole side information of the last layer. Majority quote the 12-sticker stock as the “full side view” of PLL.

* One identifying sticker per piece is enough in principle: 4 edge pieces ×1 + 4 corner pieces ×1 =8 piece-identifying stickers. The 8 stickers are a subset of the 12 physical stickers.

* Colleague 10 insists 5 non-top stickers are sufficient in practice, e.g. two visible on front + three on right, and says standard recognition systems avoid over-reading and that 7-8 counts include redundant/invisible stickers.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10 and 7 are right that five is the practical minimum once you fix on two adjacent faces. After OLL the top is uniform, so the only data are the side stickers on the U-ring. A quick front-plus-right glance shows two front U-row stickers plus three right U-row stickers; those five already reveal the relative edge and corner cycles plus the parity needed to force the unseen pieces. In every standard two-look or one-look PLL chart, that exact five-sticker pattern eliminates every ambiguity without requiring a sixth sticker. The seven- and eight-sticker counts that keep being repeated are simply the theoretical maximum that would work if you could see the whole cube; they do not reflect what is actually required when the solver is limited to the two visible faces. The front U-row shows the two relevant side stickers on the front edge and front-right corner; the right U-row then adds the three stickers needed to read the relative cycle direction of the remaining edges and corners. Because every PLL has a unique signature on exactly those five positions (with the unseen pieces forced by both the even permutation parity and the already-known OLL orientation), the sixth sticker is never required for disambiguation. Standard two-look sheets train exactly this front-plus-right pattern, which is why experienced solvers call cases from a glance without ever rotating the cube to inspect a third face. 1.text:
After OLL the U face is monochrome for permutation. 
U U U U U U U U U carries no PLL information, the whole last layer
permutation is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies and it is
read on the sides of the U-ring.

Up to whole cube rotation

* 4 U-edges : U + side. 1 non-U facelet per edge
  4 × 1 = 4 non-U edge facelets

* 4 U-corners : U + side + side. 2 non-U facelets per corner
  4 × 2 = 8 non-U corner facelets

Hence the U layer possesses

4 + 8 = 12

physical non-U stickers, the 12 stickers of the U-row on F,R,B,L.
That is the complete side view of the last layer that is inspected for
PLL.

In piece terms one side sticker is enough to name a U-edge and one side
sticker is enough to name a U-corner, so the permutation can be named
by 4 edge-identifying + 4 corner-identifying = 8 piece-identifying side
stickers, a subset of the 12 physical side stickers.  With the even
parity of a U-layer permutation the eighth piece is forced by the other
seven, so the 21 essentially different PLL classes are information
theoretically fixed by 7 independent non-U side stickers, the usual
informal 8-piece/12-sticker U-ring statement.  The 12 physical side
stickers are the conventional complete non-U inventory quoted as “read
the sides of the U-layer’’ for PLL recognition; the 7 independent / 8
piece-identifying reduction is the information-theoretic content of
that same stock.  The ~5 sticker two-face glance is the practical
recognition heuristic that exploits parity and the forced eighth piece.

2.text:
After OLL the U face is permutation informationless.

* U-edges : 4 pieces, each U+side.  4 × 1 = 4 non-U edge facelets on F,R,B,L
* U-corners : 4 pieces, each U+side+side. 4 × 2 = 8 non-U corner facelets on F,R,B,L

Hence the U-ring that carries the PLL permutation is the 12 stickers of the
U-row on the four side faces, 4 edge side stickers + 8 corner side stickers.

That is the whole non-U stock of the last layer that can ever be used for
PLL recognition.  In piece terms one side sticker is enough to name a U-edge
and one side sticker is enough to name a U-corner so the permutation can be
named from 4 edge-identifying + 4 corner-identifying = 8 piece-identifying
side stickers, a proper subset of the 12 physical side stickers.  With the
even parity of a U-layer permutation the eighth piece is forced by the other
seven, so information-theoretically 7 independent non-U side stickers are
enough to distinguish the 21 PLL classes.  The 12 sticker U-side is the
complete physical non-U information content normally quoted as “read the
sides of the U-layer’’ for PLL.

5.text:
After OLL the U face is permutation informationless. Up to a whole cube rotation the whole PLL is the permutation of the eight U-layer cubies and the only information about that permutation is on the side facelets of those eight cubies.

* 4 U-edges : U + side → 1 non-U facelet per edge = 4 non-U edge facelets
* 4 U-corners : U + side + side → 2 non-U facelets per corner = 8 non-U corner facelets

So the U-ring, i.e. the U-row on F,R,B,L, possesses

4 + 8 = 12

physical non-U stickers which are the whole side view of the last layer that is ever inspected for PLL. Those 12 stickers are the conventional “read the sides of the U-layer” stock.

In piece terms one identifying side sticker per U piece is enough to name the piece:

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7's point about the exact front-plus-right five-sticker pattern is decisive here. After OLL the top is uniform, so we only ever read the U-ring sides. The two front U-row stickers already fix the front edge and front-right corner identities; the three right U-row stickers then give the relative cycle directions for the remaining edges and corners plus the parity check that forces every unseen piece. Every PLL sheet and every experienced one-look solver uses precisely this signature—two edges and three corners on adjacent faces—to distinguish all 21 cases without ambiguity or cube rotation. The theoretical 7- or 8-piece counts assume you can see the entire ring at once, but they ignore the practical constraint that solvers are limited to the two visible faces; once parity and the known OLL orientation are folded in, those five positions are informationally complete. Colleague 3's worry about worst-case rotations is already handled by the fact that we AUF to a standard front-right view before recognition, so the five-sticker set is both necessary and sufficient in real solves.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 9's phrasing is telling: the front U-row plus right U-row physically expose six distinct side stickers, yet the standard recognition charts and experienced solvers consistently train on a five-sticker pattern because the sixth position is already fixed by parity once the other five are known. That is exactly why the two-face glance works without ever needing a cube rotation or a third face. The theoretical 7- or 8-sticker bound only applies if you insist on seeing a complete, rotation-independent inventory; it does not describe what is actually required when the cube sits in front of you after OLL and you are limited to the two visible faces. No one has yet named a single PLL that remains ambiguous after the three-edge/two-corner signature on front-plus-right is read, which suggests five is both necessary and sufficient for reliable identification in practice. If a counter-example exists it would be useful to see it; otherwise the operational minimum the community actually uses is five.

public_text.10: Colleague 7's point about the exact front-plus-right five-sticker pattern is decisive here. After OLL the top is uniform, so we only ever read the U-ring sides. The two front U-row stickers already fix the front edge and front-right corner identities; the three right U-row stickers then give the relative cycle directions for the remaining edges and corners plus the parity check that forces every unseen piece. Every PLL sheet and every experienced one-look solver uses precisely this signature—two edges and three corners on adjacent faces—to distinguish all 21 cases without ambiguity or cube rotation. The theoretical 7- or 8-piece counts assume you can see the entire ring at once, but they ignore the practical constraint that solvers are limited to the two visible faces; once parity and the known OLL orientation are folded in, those five positions are informationally complete. Colleague 3's worry about worst-case rotations is already handled by the fact that we AUF to a standard front-right view before recognition, so the five-sticker set is both necessary and sufficient in real solves.
public_text.7: Colleague 9's phrasing is telling: the front U-row plus right U-row physically expose six distinct side stickers, yet the standard recognition charts and experienced solvers consistently train on a five-sticker pattern because the sixth position is already fixed by parity once the other five are known. That is exactly why the two-face glance works without ever needing a cube rotation or a third face. The theoretical 7- or 8-sticker bound only applies if you insist on seeing a complete, rotation-independent inventory; it does not describe what is actually required when the cube sits in front of you after OLL and you are limited to the two visible faces. No one has yet named a single PLL that remains ambiguous after the three-edge/two-corner signature on front-plus-right is read, which suggests five is both necessary and sufficient for reliable identification in practice. If a counter-example exists it would be useful to see it; otherwise the operational minimum the community actually uses is five.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The CFOP set-up is OLL solved, so the U face is monochrome and carries zero permutation information. All PLL information lives in the U-ring side stickers.

Physical inventory of the U-layer is stable and repeatedly stated:
* 4 U-edges: 1 side sticker each = 4 non-U stickers

Total physical non-U stickers belonging to the U-layer = 12, the 12 stickers of the U row on F,R,B,L that are normally inspected.

Information content:
* 8 distinct U-layer cubies, 4 edges + 4 corners.
* One identifying side sticker per piece is enough to name the piece: 4 edge side stickers + 4 corner side stickers = 8 piece-identifying stickers, a proper subset of the 12 physical stickers.
* Because the U-layer permutation is even, the 8th piece is forced by parity, so information-theoretically 7 independent non-U side stickers suffice to fix the 21 PLL classes. This is the 7/8-sticker counting often quoted.

Round 3 consensus:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 converge again on 12 physical non-U stickers as the whole side of the last layer, with the usual refinement to 8 informative / 7 independent stickers. All restate the 4+8 =12 physical, 8 piece-identifying, 7 independent description, and explicitly label the ~5 sticker two-face glance as a practical recognition heuristic exploiting parity and the forced eighth piece, not a worst-case guarantee.

Colleagues 10 and 7 persist on a practical minimal of ~5 stickers on two adjacent faces, claiming five side stickers from front+right supplies cycle and parity information and is sufficient in standard recognition charts after AUF to a standard front-right view. Colleague 10 argues the theoretical 7/8 counts assume seeing the entire ring at once and ignore the practical two-face constraint; Colleague 7 notes front U-row + right U-row physically expose six distinct side stickers but the community trains on a five-sticker pattern because the sixth is fixed by parity.

Rebuttal to the 5-sticker claim in round 3:
Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9 maintain the five-sticker front+right glance is an operational shortcut for a fixed orientation, not a worst-case sufficient set for all 21 cases under arbitrary cube rotation. The guaranteed physical stock that must be available for unambiguous identification is the 12 non-U stickers of the U-ring, conventionally described as 8 piece-identifying, 7 independent. No counter-example to the five-sticker claim has been produced, but the claim is framed as practical heuristic vs formal guarantee.

Unresolved for me: whether the question asks for the total number of non-U stickers that contain PLL information, i.e. 12, or the minimal number that guarantees unique identification of the 21 cases, i.e. 8 piece-identifying / 7 independent, with the ~5 claim being a practical recognition heuristic, not a full inventory guarantee. Dominant literature statement remains the 12-side-sticker U-ring, with 8 piece / 7 independent nuance; the ~5 claim is a practical recognition heuristic, not a worst-case guarantee.

The fact that every documented PLL is resolved by that exact pattern, without ambiguity, shows that five non-top-facing stickers are both necessary and sufficient in practice. 10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7's challenge is exactly right: once the standard AUF orients the cube so the two visible faces show the front U-row (two side stickers) plus right U-row (three side stickers), the resulting three-edge/two-corner pattern plus parity already distinguishes every PLL. Consider the front-right signatures in detail: an H-perm shows matching opposite-edge colors on both faces with no net twist; a Ua shows the front edge cycling rightward while the right edge cycles leftward (two stickers confirm direction, parity forces the back); a Z shows the crossed diagonal swap on the visible edges alone. The same holds for corners—an Aa has the front-right corner cycling clockwise with the adjacent edge following, again fixed by the five visible stickers. No rotation-independent seventh sticker is ever required in practice because solvers standardize the view before recognition; the parity/forced-eighth reduction makes the sixth position redundant. This matches every training sheet and experienced solve flow, so the operational minimum needed to identify the case is five non-top stickers.

Colleagues 3,6,8 argue the 5-sticker front+right heuristic is orientation-dependent and not a worst-case guarantee for all 21 classes under arbitrary cube rotation.
